title: How Smells Travel
objective: After this level you can explain how smell molecules reach your nose.
summary: Smelling is detecting airborne chemicals, so only volatile substances have a smell. Warmth frees more molecules, and diffusion spreads them in a slow zigzag because they keep colliding.

cards.headline: You can smell a pizza before you see it.
cards.body: The delivery box is still closed in the hallway, yet the smell is already in the room. Something real traveled from the pizza to your nose: molecules. Smell is the detection of chemicals carried in the air.

cards.headline: Only escapees have a smell
cards.body: If smelling means catching chemicals from the air, a substance can only have a smell if some of its molecules get into the air. Odor molecules are volatile: they vaporize readily. Anything you can smell right now is quietly sending bits of itself your way.

cards.headline: Warmth launches more molecules
cards.body: Remember Level 4: heating makes particles move faster. As a liquid warms, more of its molecules have enough energy to escape into the air. So a steaming bowl of soup sends more smell molecules into the room than the same soup straight from the fridge.

cards.headline: Fast molecules, slow journey
cards.body: Gas molecules zip along at hundreds of meters per second. So why does a smell take time to cross a room? Each molecule keeps colliding with other molecules and bouncing off in a new direction. The overall spreading, from where molecules are crowded to where they're sparse, is called diffusion. It's a zigzag commute, not a sprint.

mascot.line: Imagine crossing a crowded party by bumping into every guest. That's a smell molecule's evening.

cards.headline: Smell: traced
learned: Smell is detecting chemicals carried in the air
Odor molecules are volatile: they vaporize readily
Warmth frees more molecules into the air
Diffusion spreads them in a slow zigzag of collisions

questions.prompt: What is the name for smell molecules spreading from where they're crowded to where they're sparse?

options.label: Distillation
options.rationale: That's separating liquids by boiling point.

options.label: Condensation
options.rationale: That's a gas turning into a liquid.

options.label: Filtration
options.rationale: That's holding back solids with a filter.

questions.explanation: Diffusion is molecules spreading out from where they're concentrated to where they're not.

questions.prompt: Smell molecules move at hundreds of meters per second. Why does a smell still take time to cross a room?

options.label: They slow down to rest along the way
options.rationale: They keep moving fast; collisions steer them.

options.label: They must turn back into a liquid first
options.rationale: They travel as a gas the whole way.

options.label: Air is too cold for molecules to move
options.rationale: Air molecules are moving too, and that's the problem.

options.label: They keep colliding and changing direction

questions.explanation: Constant collisions send each molecule zigzagging, so the overall spread is much slower than the molecules' speed.

questions.prompt: Using Level 4's idea that heat speeds up particles, why does warm soup smell stronger than cold soup?

options.label: Heat adds new ingredients to the soup
options.rationale: The soup is the same; more of it reaches the air.

options.label: More molecules have enough energy to escape into the air
Cold soup has no smell molecules in it
Heat destroys the smell molecules
options.rationale: Then warm soup would smell weaker, not stronger.

questions.explanation: Warming gives more molecules the energy to escape into the air, so more of them reach your nose.
